questions.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $Y$ if the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y},\, & y\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $Y$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(Y\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le m) & ={\int }_{0}^{m}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-y}{|}_{0}^{m} \\  & =1-{e}^{-m}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ -m & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{1}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =4 \\ {q}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{3}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =12 \\ {q}_{3} & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
IQR={q}_{3}-{q}_{1}=2\sqrt{3}-2≈1.464
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
Find the $60$th percentile of the random variable $Y$ if the probability distribution function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}},\, & y\ge 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $Y$ is the number ${y}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(Y\le {y}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $60$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.6.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le {y}_{0.6}) & ={\int }_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={-\frac{1}{y}|}_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $60$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.6 \\ \frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.4 \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{1}{0.4} \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the $72.9$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{x},\, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $72.9$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.729.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.729}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $72.9$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8} & =0.729 \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =\sqrt[3]{(8)(0.729)} \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =(2)(0.9) \\ {x}_{0.729} & =(1.8)^{2} \\ {x}_{0.729} & =3.24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1, \\ 1-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{3}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{1}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\sqrt[6]{4}-\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$
